text: Before features, start with billing, because it genuinely changes the whole economics of this decision. Azure Data Factory bills pay-as-you-go, per activity run, data movement, and compute. Fabric Data Factory runs against purchased capacity, an F SKU, with no separate charge for external or pipeline activities themselves — only activity runs and data movement.

If your organization already owns Fabric capacity for Power BI or other workloads, Fabric Data Factory pipelines can run against capacity you're already paying for. If you're purely doing data movement with no other real Fabric usage, ADF's pay-as-you-go model may genuinely be simpler to reason about and budget for.

Roughly ninety percent of ADF's activities are available in Fabric today, plus some genuinely Fabric-only additions like Outlook and Teams activities. Notice that number isn't a hundred — Fabric isn't a strict superset of ADF yet. If your pipeline genuinely depends on that remaining ten percent, SSIS execution being the biggest single piece of it, that alone can decide the question for you.

Stay on classic ADF if you run real SSIS packages, need ADF's fully Microsoft-managed virtual network with zero setup, or your organization has no Fabric capacity at all. Move to Fabric if your destination is already a Lakehouse or Warehouse, you already own Fabric capacity, or you want business users comfortable with Power Query helping build real transformations. And it's genuinely not always either-or — the mounted-ADF-item path lets both run side by side indefinitely, not just as a migration stepping stone.

That closes out Chapter Nine: the Fabric stack, Dataflow Gen2, pipelines re-imagined, OneLake, migration paths, and now the real decision framework tying it all together. Next, Chapter Ten: Security, DevOps and CI/CD — managed identities, Key Vault, and getting pipelines into genuine production.
